title: The rababis
hook: Muslim musicians descended from Mardana's tradition sang the Gurus' hymns at the Harmandir for generations

segments.voice: Yesterday, gurdwaras abroad, in cities far from Punjab. Your line was the guru abroad. Did you look one up, and was it closer than you expected? Day one thousand three hundred forty-two.

A wooden instrument with a rounded belly, a skin face, and strings that buzz low under a singing voice. That's a rabab. In the janamsakhi stories, Guru Nanak sings and a Muslim companion named Mardana plays a rabab beside him, village after village, road after road. The Guru sings; the rabab answers. Tradition says Mardana's music didn't end with Mardana. Families of Muslim musicians kept the craft, and for generations they sang the Gurus' hymns at the Harmandir in Amritsar, until the partition of Punjab drew a border through their lives. Those singers have a name, and it's today's word.
screen: `A RABAB: SKIN, WOOD, LOW STRINGS.` → `MARDANA PLAYS; THE GURU SINGS.` → `THE MUSIC PASSED DOWN.`

segments.voice: First, the name. A rababi is simply a rabab player, and the word became the name for these families of Muslim kirtan singers. They sang Sikh scripture in the ragas it's written in, a calling passed from parent to child. Second, a place inside the book. The Guru Granth Sahib holds a ballad credited to two minstrels, Satta and Balwand, in Raag Ramkali. It praises the Gurus, and the light passing from one Guru to the next. Tradition remembers Satta and Balwand as musicians at the Gurus' court. So the musicians who served the Gurus aren't only remembered beside the scripture. Some of their words sit inside it, sung in gurdwaras today. Third, what the border did. As rababi families remember it, when Punjab was divided they went west, to the new Pakistan, and the music they had carried into the Harmandir went with them. Their kind of kirtan was heard less and less on the Amritsar side. Some Sikhs speak of that as a real loss, and some musicians, Sikh and Muslim, have worked to bring the rabab back into kirtan. Fourth, the shape of the whole story. A Guru walks the roads with a Muslim friend and an instrument. The friend's heirs, Muslims too, keep singing the Guru's words for generations at the Harmandir. Nobody in that story had to stop being who they were to sing together. That's the picture to keep: a faith whose hymns, in its own stories, were carried on a Muslim musician's strings. Mardana's heirs.
screen: `RABABI: A RABAB PLAYER.` · `SATTA AND BALWAND: INSIDE THE BOOK.` · `A BORDER, AND A LOSS.` · `A MUSLIM FRIEND'S STRINGS.` · then, large: `MARDANA'S HEIRS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to rabab music. Settle, and breathe. If you can, find a recording of the rabab, or of kirtan sung with one, and let it play quietly. If you can't right now, recall any low, plucked string you've ever heard. Listen for the place where the instrument and the voice meet and lean on each other. Then think of who stands behind the sound: the player, the one who taught the player, and the one who taught them. Breathe in with the music. Breathe out with it. The bell holds the time.
Rababi. A rabab player: the name for the families of Muslim musicians who, tradition says, sang the Gurus' hymns at the Harmandir for generations. Today's word.
Your line: mardana's heirs. Today, when a piece of music reaches you, think of the people who carried it to you, and name one if you can. Day one thousand three hundred forty-two.

howItsDone: Kirtan in gurdwaras is usually led by Sikh raagis today; a small number of musicians, Sikh and Muslim, keep rabab playing and the rababi way of singing alive in performance and recordings.

notes: The index hook names 1947; per the claims rule the year is not spoken and the hook field reads 'for generations'. The script says the rababis sang at the Harmandir 'until the partition of Punjab drew a border through their lives' and that families 'went west, to the new Pakistan'. Please confirm this is fairly put.
The rababis as descendants of Mardana's tradition is given as 'tradition says'; please confirm how strongly to state lineage from Mardana.
Satta and Balwand's var in Raag Ramkali: Ang 966–968 cited from memory; please confirm the Ang range and that they are fairly called minstrels/musicians at the Gurus' court.
'Some musicians, Sikh and Muslim, have worked to bring the rabab back into kirtan' is a general claim; please confirm or soften.
Rabab described as having 'a rounded belly, a skin face' and low strings; please confirm for the Sikh/Punjabi rabab (sometimes called the Firandia rabab).
Editor: the partition move is now framed as the rababi families' own memory rather than a flat historical claim; the rest stands.
